vignette:
She is 23, a South Asian woman who now works as an auditor, and when she talks about the year the fighting reached her neighborhood, she does so in a voice that stays level for a while before suddenly going flat. She says that before the war moved close, her life had felt ordinary in the way she misses most now: commuting to classes, helping her mother prepare dinner, complaining about exams, making plans with friends she assumed she would always have. Then the shelling began to sound nearer each week. At first her family tried to continue as if routine itself could hold the world together. They kept the lights low at night, learned which windows were safest, and followed rumors about which roads were still open. She remembers the strange split in her mind during those weeks—part of her still noticing small details, like the smell of cardamom in the kitchen, while another part stayed alert to every distant boom.

The night that stays with her most vividly began with a noise she first took for thunder. It was not thunder. The building shook hard enough to throw a glass from the table. Her mother screamed for everyone to get down. She remembers the pressure in her chest, the dust in the air, and her younger cousin crying so hard he could not catch his breath. There were explosions close by, then shouting in the street, then the crack of gunfire that sounded impossibly casual, as if it belonged to another world. They spent hours crowded in a hallway away from the windows. At some point a nearby building was hit. She says she knew this not because she saw it happen, but because of the scream that followed—a sound she still hears at night, detached from any face, somehow worse because of that.

In the days after, her family left home with only what they could carry. She tells this part quickly, but her hands tighten in her lap: checkpoints, men with rifles, roads lined with damaged cars, the smell of smoke everywhere. She saw a body on the roadside and tried not to look, then hated herself for not looking. At a temporary shelter she slept sitting up, waking at every footstep. If someone dropped a metal tray, her whole body jerked before she knew why. She began to scan every room automatically for exits and sturdy walls. Even when there was a lull in the fighting, she could not believe in it. She learned that calm was only what came before the next blast.

When she eventually relocated, she told herself survival required moving forward. She finished her education, found work in auditing, and became known for being meticulous. At the office she is dependable, precise, and almost unnaturally prepared. She checks figures repeatedly, catches minor inconsistencies others miss, and keeps color-coded notes that colleagues admire. She knows some of this is skill and discipline. She also knows some of it comes from the same relentless vigilance that once kept her alive. She cannot tolerate uncertainty in spreadsheets, timelines, or meeting agendas. Unexpected changes make her heart race in a way she tries hard to hide.

Her days are organized around preventing distress she rarely names aloud. She avoids news footage, especially anything with sirens, rubble, or crowds running. She no longer goes to fireworks displays and pretends she finds them childish. If construction starts outside her office window, she loses the thread of conversations and has to excuse herself to the restroom, where she stands in a stall breathing through nausea and shame. At night she sleeps lightly. Some nights she dreams she is back in the hallway, unable to move her family to safety; other nights there are no images, only the feeling of impending impact, and she wakes already panicked. In the morning she is exhausted but unwilling to admit how little rest she gets.

She is single and keeps most relationships at a careful distance. Friends describe her as kind but hard to know. When people ask about where she is from, she offers polished, factual answers that reveal nothing of what she saw. She feels detached in moments that are supposed to be joyful, as if some essential part of her never fully came forward from that hallway. Loud laughter from strangers can make her flinch if she mistakes it for shouting. A slammed door can ruin the next hour. In crowded trains she positions herself near exits and watches everyone who comes in. She hates this about herself and also cannot stop.

What troubles her almost as much as fear is the guilt. She thinks of neighbors who did not get out, of friends she lost touch with and later learned were dead, of how her own life now contains office deadlines and coffee orders while theirs ended in smoke and concrete. She feels ungrateful for being unhappy when she survived. Still, she moves through the present as if disaster is not past but pending. She performs competence expertly, arrives early, meets deadlines, answers emails, and keeps her desk immaculate. Beneath that, her body remains braced, her sleep fractured, her attention pulled backward by sounds and memories she never chose to keep.
